title: Feathers in the Wind
text:
In a small town a man spread a story about the local rabbi. It was not true, but it was interesting, and it passed from mouth to mouth through the market and the houses until everyone had heard it.

After a while the man began to feel ashamed. He went to the rabbi, admitted what he had done, and asked how he could make amends. He was ready to do whatever penance was required.

The rabbi told him to take a feather pillow, carry it to the top of a hill, cut it open and shake the feathers out into the wind. Then he was to come back. The man thought this an easy penance. He did as he was told, watched the feathers swirl away over the roofs and fields, and returned to the rabbi, relieved.

"Now," said the rabbi, "go and gather up all the feathers."

The man protested that it was impossible. The wind had already carried them everywhere, over walls, into gardens and far across the fields. "Exactly," said the rabbi. "And that is how it is with the words you spread. You can ask forgiveness, but you can never gather them all back."
lesson: Think before repeating a story about someone. Once words are out, no apology can follow every place they reach.
source: Jewish folk tradition, told of several Hasidic rabbis
caveat: The tale has no single original source and is attributed to various rabbis in different versions.
